en: Commentary on the Heart Sutra by the Wayman Without Dependence (Wuyi Daoren), Xu Changzhi, son of Jin Zhou;
with his sons Xu Shengzhen, Xu Qianzhen, Xu Gongshu, and Xu Yizhen, who together collated [the text].
The *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* is its Sanskrit title.
*Prajñā* means wisdom; it is the fundamental mind of human beings, transcending emotions and departing from views—a designation for profound stillness and perfect enlightenment.
*Pāramitā* means "reaching the other shore. *Sūtra* refers to sentient beings. "Mind" (*hṛdaya*) refers to the person.
Mind, Sutra, and Constant; these are the Dharmas. Mind is the essence of prajñā, while prajñā is the function of mind.
The "other shore" (pāra) is the actual realm reached within the mind of prajñā.
Regarding the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara:

"Observation" (avalokita) has two meanings. First, there is the observing wisdom (*avalokana-jñāna*), which is the subject; second, there are the observed characteristics (*avalokita-lakṣaṇa*), which are the objects.

The harmonious realization of subject and object is termed "sovereignty" (*īśvara*). Because he guides sentient beings by means of this principle of harmonious realization, he is called a "Bodhisattva."

Because all sentient beings falsely perceive reality and fail to turn back from it, they give rise to the three poisons and create various karmas, transmigrating through the three realms, rising and falling, ascending and descending.
Throughout kalpas, there is none who attains mastery. Only this Bodhisattva realizes that all phenomena are empty;

with object and wisdom in a state of suchness (*tathatā*), though dwelling in birth and death, he is not bound by the roots of birth and death, and though dwelling in nirvana, [he does not cling to it].
"Not bound by the fruit of nirvana. "Self" (zì) reveals that every single thing and every single instance is none other than one's own self.
"Present" (zài) reveals that every dust mote and every buddha-field is everywhere pervasive.
When practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the "practitioner" (*yogin*) refers to the practice that is cultivated; "profound *prajñā*" refers to the wisdom that is realized and verified;
and "time" (*kāla*) refers to the moment when both subject and object are forgotten and both wisdom and principle are extinguished. This *prajñā* is formless.
It is signless; it has no direction and no location; it is neither internal nor external; it is boundless and unmanifest; it admits of no deliberation or conjecture.
Therefore, it is called "profound. The character "time" (時) refers back to the period prior to vast eons.
Once one attains correspondence with this from the very beginning, one will continue until the end of the future limit, never departing from the profound Prajñā from start to finish.
"To perceive that the five aggregates are all empty, and thereby transcend all suffering and affliction.
This explains how the aforementioned Bodhisattva entered into the profound *prajñā*. By what means was this achieved? It was through a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*).
That which is reached by vision is called the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). The experiencing of what is seen is called the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).
The incessant conceptualization is called the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). The shifting and flowing [of mental states] is called the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

The discerning and judging [of objects] is called the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). These five are hidden and submerged, binding the human mind; therefore, they are called "aggregates" (*skandha*). All of these are suffering.
"Calamity" (*ē*) refers to sentient beings. It means that a Bodhisattva who is able to cultivate Prajñā has a self-mind that is pure and perfectly interfused, lacking even the slightest obstruction;
thus, they are able to deliver worldly sentient beings who possess obstructions and hindrances and are subject to suffering and calamity.
The character for "mind" (*xīn*) is depicted in its entirety, yet the character for "mind" is not explicitly revealed; this is why it is so.
Exquisite!
All five aggregates (*skandhas*) are originally pure, eternally abiding within the one mind, and are fundamentally the true emptiness of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
To guard the mouth, restrain the mind, and not let the body commit transgressions is also a dharma for transcending the world. This is also the case for the three vehicles that transcend the world.

Nevertheless, based upon the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), one establishes the distinctions of depth and shallowness in their refutation. Apart from the five aggregates, there are no dharmas of the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
Ordinary beings lack wisdom and are bound by the five aggregates; those of the two vehicles have shallow wisdom and are bound by the emptiness of annihilation (*uccheda-śūnyatā*). [The profound...]
Prajñā clearly perceives that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are originally empty by nature. Thus, the five aggregates are detached from the five aggregates;
it is not necessary to eliminate the five aggregates before one can see their emptiness. These five aggregates are suffering (*duḥkha*). Since the five aggregates are empty...
Who is it that suffers?
Śāriputra, form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form. Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form.
Regarding the name Śāri, in the Sanskrit language it means "partridge. This is because this Venerable One’s mother had eyes as sharp as those of a partridge bird.
"Eye" (*mukha*): This was used by people of the time as a term of praise and acclaim. The Venerable One derived his name from his mother; thus he was called Śāriputra.
Among the *śrāvakas*, this Venerable One was foremost in wisdom. Because his wisdom was capable of entering into the *prajñāpāramitā*, the World-Honored One specifically summoned and addressed him.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara perceived that the five aggregates are all empty. This is not because the aggregates are themselves the aggregates and emptiness is itself emptiness;
rather, they are of one essence and identical. Form (*rūpa*) is the foremost of dharmic characteristics and the first of the five aggregates;
therefore, whenever various sutras wish to explain the meaning of emptiness, they do so by means of form. This is because form is solid and substantial.

Deluded thoughts coalesce and solidify; this is the point where sentient beings most easily become attached. Second, they stand in diametric opposition to the essence and characteristics of empty space;
this is the most difficult point to reconcile. If one can penetrate and break through this, then the remaining four aggregates will disintegrate like crumbling walls and melt away like ice.
As it is said: "Once one sense-faculty returns to its source, all six sense-faculties achieve liberation."

Furthermore, the followers of the Hīnayāna regard form as substantial, perceiving it as distinct from the voidness of emptiness; they thus see that form can obstruct emptiness and that emptiness is hindered by form.
The Bodhisattva, however, perceives that all forms are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This lack of intrinsic nature—
Form is itself the principle of non-self and emptiness. From the very beginning, not even a single thread or speck can be found that can stain or defile emptiness;

nor can one find even a single thread or speck that can be mixed with or intermingled with emptiness. The characteristic of form and the characteristic of emptiness are from the outset without distinction;
therefore, it is said they are not different.
The followers of the two vehicles and bodhisattvas at the initial stage perceive emptiness as annihilation, distinct from the defilement of form;

they consequently seek to extinguish form to realize emptiness, whereby form becomes an obstacle to emptiness. Bodhisattvas, however, perceive that the self-nature of form is empty, and thus it is true emptiness.
Pervading the entire dharma-realm, this principle of selflessness and emptiness is omnipresent within all form.
One does not perceive any defiled form existing outside of emptiness, nor does one perceive any form within emptiness that can be severed or extinguished.
The essence of emptiness and the essence of form are entirely without change; therefore, it is said that they are "identical.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
This uses the four aggregates to infer by analogy that the preceding aggregate of form all arise from conditions. As for what is called "feeling":
Its nature is that of experiencing. It experiences three types of objects—those that are favorable, unfavorable, or neutral—all of which lack substantial reality.

If it experiences what is favorable, it will ultimately possess a favorable nature; when encountering an unfavorable object, it would logically not arise [as such]. Thus, one knows that feeling (*vedanā*) is itself empty.

As for the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), it likewise lacks substantial reality. If it perceives a preceding object, and that preceding object possessed substantial reality, it would no longer...
After the perception [of form], one again perceives what follows it; thus one knows it has no substance. How could this be anything other than emptiness?

As for what is called the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), it shifts and passes away from moment to moment and possesses no real nature. If this nature were within, it should not shift to the outside; if the nature were outside, [it would not be within].
One should not conceive of them as migrating internally; thus we know that there is nothing to be attained, whether internal or external. If they are not empty, what are they?

As for what is called the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), consciousness is threefold: first, the *ālaya-vijñāna*; second, the *manas-vijñāna*; and third, the consciousness that cognizes objects.

These three consciousnesses are by nature fundamentally void; they arise and perish in alternation, having originally no existence that can be apprehended. If they are not empty, what are they? This is what is meant by the five...
That all aggregates are empty is thus. It is not apart from the five aggregates that the five aggregates are empty.
Can a bodhisattva who practices profound *prajñā* and reaches the other shore do otherwise?
Śāriputra, these dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness: they are neither born nor extinguished; neither defiled nor pure; neither increasing nor decreasing.
Tracing back the preceding aggregates, one finds that dependent origination has no substantial essence. This directly brings one back to one's own mind.
Although this sutra reveals the mind as primary, it does not yet employ the word "mind."
The preceding passage has already explained that the five aggregates are all empty. Fearing that people might fail to grasp this and mistake it for a mere peripheral practice of contemplation,
rather than believing in the primordially inherent nature of the true mark (*dharmatā*), I shall now point out the characteristic of emptiness within all phenomena,
so that you may know the original true mark.
Ordinarily, viewing form and emptiness as opposites is not understood to be the very self-characteristic of True Suchness (tathatā).
Therefore, he again addressed Śāriputra, saying: "The five aggregates are empty. In reality, this applies not only to the five aggregates.
All dharmas are, in their very nature, empty. All dharmas arise from conditions; that which arises from conditions lacks intrinsic nature.
In reality, dharmas are fundamentally unarisen. When the conditions for dharmas depart, they cease; yet this cessation is merely the cessation of conditions.
In reality, dharmas are fundamentally unceasing. They are neither arising nor ceasing. Although they exist within tainted form, their essence is empty and non-existent.
Although it exists within untainted form (*anāsravarūpa*), its essence as emptiness remains as it was; it is neither defiled nor pure.
This mark of emptiness of all phenomena has never been reached through cultivation or realization; since its virtue is full, it does not increase.
Since it is primordially subject to transformation and decay, yet cannot be so affected, and since its obstructions are exhausted, yet not extinguished, it is neither increasing nor decreasing.
Therefore, in emptiness there is no form; no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
There is no form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or phenomenon. There is no realm of the eye, and so on, up to and including no realm of mental consciousness.
This uses the five aggregates, the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the twelve bases to reveal true emptiness.
It brings the dependent origination of all phenomena back to one's own mind, yet it does not explicitly state that this is the mind.
The eye-faculty, through the two objects of light and darkness, mutually attracts and draws one another; by removing deluded seeing, its original clarity is restored, wherein nothing at all exists.
The ear-faculty, through the two objects of movement and stillness, mutually encompasses and supports one another; by removing deluded hearing, [its original clarity is restored].
Return to their original clarity, which is entirely non-existent. The nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, and the body-faculty all arise from and perish with various sensory objects;
they separate and unite of their own accord. Eliminate their deluded cognition and return to their fundamental state, which is entirely non-existent. The mind-faculty...
Through the entering and exiting of the two types of objects, their mutual arising and subsiding eliminate delusive thoughts and restore original enlightenment, such that nothing at all exists.
Furthermore, the six sense-objects arise from the differentiation between the faculties and consciousness;

that is to say, if one listens through the ears, it is ultimately difficult to comprehend, whereas by hearing sound within the eyes, one finally attains knowledge. When the body is at ease and the mind is content, every point of contact is tranquil. The faculties—

When both sensory objects (*viṣaya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are absent, from what could the realms (*dhātu*) be established? For those whose delusion regarding the mind is predominant, the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are taught;

for those whose delusion regarding form is predominant, the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) are taught; and for those whose delusion regarding both form and mind is predominant, the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*) are taught.

These three categories, when they exist, constitute the karmic obstructions of the three realms of existence (*tribhava*); when they do not exist, all phenomena are empty. As for the "three realms," there are three... [text fragment].
The world is also the three realms: namely, the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. The five aggregates are merely the two characters "form" and "mind.
The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, as well as forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, constitute the dharmas of form; the mind constitutes the dharma of mind.
The true emptiness of Buddha-nature has two kinds of function: first, the function of its own nature; second, the function of following conditions. For example:
A bright mirror hangs empty; it does not inquire whether objects arrive or not. That the mirror’s radiance possesses the capacity for manifestation is called the "function of self-nature.
When an object suddenly arrives, the mirror manifests its form accordingly; this is called the "function of following conditions.

Regarding the twelve *āyatanas*, because the internal faculties and external objects each have their own locations, the six consciousnesses differentiate the six sense-objects, clinging to delusions and forming distinctions. Each...

There is a limit; it is called the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*). Although the three groups of six are presented together, the emphasis lies on the six consciousnesses. The six consciousnesses are fundamentally but a single consciousness.
There is no ignorance, nor is there the exhaustion of ignorance; likewise, there is no old age and death, nor is there the exhaustion of old age and death.
Continuing from what was said above: all people have both clarity and lack of clarity; these are merely the burdens imposed by the visual faculty (*cakṣur-dhātu*).

Once the visual faculty is empty and clarity reaches its ultimate limit, how could there be ignorance (*avidyā*) that does not reach that same limit? Upon reaching this state, one finally realizes the true, empty nature of the eye.
Birth, old age, sickness, and death are the most entangling fetters within the mind, from which one cannot yet detach one's emotions.
As for the sphere: since the sphere of mental consciousness is empty, it reaches the limit where birth ceases. Why then would old age and death not reach that same limit?
Upon reaching this point, one realizes the true, empty nature of the mind itself.
Within true emptiness, there is primordial, constant awareness. When aware, one is unmoving; even when movement occurs, it is originally and inherently unmoving.
It is a pure, great treasury of radiant light—how could ignorance possibly exist therein?

From the formations of consciousness up to old age and death, they arise in their own place and perish in that very place. There is no object to be conditioned, and their arising is fundamentally without arising. Primordially...
In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, even the body of the six sense faculties does not exist; how then could there be aging and death, such that one could speak of the exhaustion of aging and death?
There is no suffering, origin, cessation, or path.

Suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) pertain to the causes and effects of the mundane world. Cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) pertain to the causes and effects of the supramundane. Regarding the causes and effects of the mundane world:

the origin is the nature of being summoned and experienced, while suffering is the nature of oppression. Through greed, hatred, and delusion, one summons and experiences retributive karma, which results in oppression.
This nature of oppression does not exceed the eight types of suffering; this is what the śrāvakas understand.
Suffering. One then cultivates the path of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, and enters the extinction of nirvana.
Since the twelve links of dependent origination are themselves the Great Treasury of Radiance, how could there be any flow and cessation, or various distinctions and sequences?

For those of middling and inferior faculties, it is necessary to speak of suffering before they feel dread, to speak of cessation before they feel joy, and to speak of the origin [of suffering] before they feel...
One feels weary [of saṃsāra] and speaks of the path as that which is to be cultivated; therefore, the Dharma of the Four Truths is taught. This is the most expedient among all expedients.
If, however, it were within the true nature of emptiness, then birth and death would be the Dharmakāya, karmic fetters would be liberation, and afflictions would be prajñā.
What accumulation of suffering is there that can be weary of and renounced? Furthermore, what cessation or path is there that can be cultivated and realized?
Even the Four Noble Truths are non-existent.
That all four are called "truths" (satya) is because the Tathāgata’s words are true and forever unchanging. Thus he spoke these four.
Regarding the sequence of first the fruit and later the cause: it is intended to lead sentient beings to know suffering and sever its origin, and to delight in cessation and aspire to the Path;
only then can they depart from suffering and attain happiness.
"There is no ignorance, nor is there attainment.
World-Honored One, this directly summarizes the preceding intent by means of "no ignorance" and "no attainment. It begins with the aggregates and emptiness.
Exert yourself in contemplation; yet you still perceive the existence of dharmas and marks.

When you reach the point where the realms of sense-faculties, objects, and consciousness are entirely severed, and suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are all extinguished, you will utterly forget both self and world, and mind and environment will merge into one. This is true emptiness and ultimate truth.
Its wondrous response is inexhaustible. Furthermore, how could one know that *prajñā* possesses wisdom, or that there is something attained through the deliverance from all suffering and calamity?
One knows that both the wisdom of emptiness and the principle of emptiness that is known are both unattainable; thus it is said: "no wisdom, no attainment."
Because there is nothing to be apprehended.
This phrase connects the preceding section to the following.
Because the Bodhisattva relies on the Prajñāpāramitā, the mind is without hindrance. Because there is no hindrance...
"Without fear, far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, one attains ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
Here, for the first time, the single character 'mind' (*citta*) is revealed; this is what is meant by 'concluding [the teaching] back to one's own mind.

This is because what was extensively elucidated previously—the dependent origination of phenomena—is precisely the *prajñā* of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, wherein nothing at all is attained. Therefore, it is said: 'By means of non-attainment...'"
Therefore, by relying on this prajñā of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the bodhisattva perfectly realizes their own mind, understanding it without remainder. Hence it is said:
"By relying on the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), the mind is without hindrance. Furthermore, this mind does not abide for even a single moment.
Like a great mass of jewels, not even a hair’s breadth remains; like a flash of lightning, there is no room for deliberation.
There is not a single thing that can act as an obstruction. When the mental phenomena (*cittadharma*) are thus pure, why would fear not be eliminated?
Why would delusion (*viparyāsa*) not be cast far away? What dream could cause confusion? How could *nirvāṇa* not be attained? Such is its sovereignty.
Why is this so? A bodhisattva is the person who relies [upon it], while the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is the dharma upon which one relies.
Regarding this non-apprehension of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the Bodhisattva clings to these words.

Form and emptiness, arising and ceasing, purity and defilement, increase and decrease, the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*), as well as conditions, truths, wisdom, and attainment—all such various phenomena are but mental constructs that obstruct the mind.
Only when Prajñā illuminates true emptiness and reaches the state of non-apprehension does everything become vast and open.
There is no obstruction. What is this mastery? Contemplating to this point, the nature of karma completely vanishes.
Of all that is done, there is no doer. Relying yet having nothing to rely upon, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, everything resides within one's own radiance.
How could there be a single dharma that serves as a condition or an opponent for me? Once correct wisdom is clear, delusions naturally cease. Without cause...
Dreams vanish and return to utter purity. As it is said: "If the eyes do not sleep, all dreams naturally cease; if the mind does not diverge, the myriad dharmas are of one suchness.
When there is no fear or terror, the exhaled breath does not engage with manifold conditions, and there are no dreams or fantasies.
Then inhalation does not abide within the aggregates or the realms. As birth and cessation are both extinguished, quiescent extinction manifests before one.
Only in *nirvāṇa without remainder* is ultimate realization attained.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time, by relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Bodhi" (Enlightenment) here reveals that the Buddhas likewise realize their own minds through the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā*) and the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*śūnyatā*).
Although "Anuttara" (Unsurpassed) is a designation for the fruit [of Buddhahood], it is in fact another name for one's own mind. All phenomena reach their ultimate limit within the mind.
It is called "Unsurpassed" because there is no further distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox. It is called "Perfectly Equal" because there is no phenomenon that is not understood.

It is called "Perfect Enlightenment" because it truly awakens the nature of consciousness that was previously muddled and deluded, and is able to illuminate the great crossroads of the myriad dharmas.
Thus one knows that within the three realms there is no separate dharma; it is created solely by this one mind. Not only do Bodhisattvas cultivate and realize in this way—three...
Among all the Buddhas of the world, there are none who have not attained perfect enlightenment by relying upon Prajñā.
Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is the great divine mantra, the great illuminating mantra, and the unsurpassed mantra.
This is the peerless mantra; it can eliminate all suffering. It is true and not false. Thus [the word "thus"].

This connects directly to the preceding text, showing that the Prajñāpāramitā is the life-entrustment of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and the ultimate truth of the six hundred fascicles. How could its wondrous meaning be easily expressed? Wisdom.
By nature it subdues Māra; it is a great divine mantra. The lamp of the mind dispels darkness; it is a great illuminating mantra.
It cannot be surpassed; it is the unsurpassed mantra. There is nothing equal to it; it is the peerless mantra. Its spiritual powers are vast and its retribution is boundless.
This application of the function of Prajñā is vast and great; it eliminates suffering and attains bliss, of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, the mantra of the Prajñāpāramitā is spoken. It is spoken as follows:
*gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*.
"Gate" means "to go" or "to cross over. The repetition of "gate" signifies that one crosses over for oneself and universally crosses over others. "Pāra" means...
*Gate* means the raft of wisdom. *Pārasaṃgate* means the universal vow to ascend together to the other shore. *Bodhi svāhā* means the compassionate vessel is free from all obstructions.

When the Buddha spoke this mantra, the assembly of the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, protected and sustained it. This belongs to the secret truth (*guhyatattva*). Indeed, it is not for any purpose other than protecting the good and warding off evil.

As for "mantra" (*dhāraṇī*), it is... (Note: The source text appears to be a fragmentary commentary on the Heart Sūtra. The final term "呪者" (*zhòu zhě*) suggests the end of a definition or explanation, though the full passage is incomplete.)
This is the *praṇidhāna* (vow). May all sentient beings attain perfect enlightenment just as I have. It is also said that this refers to the name of the King of the Ghost Spirits (*piśāca-rāja*).
This sutra also possesses the three divisions [of the *nidāna*, *dharmadeśanā*, and *anuśaṃsā*].

From "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva" up to "crosses over all suffering and distress" belongs to the introductory division (*nidāna-vibhaṅga*), for it introduces the Dharma-gate by means of the Bodhisattva. [The Buddha] addressed Śāriputra...

My son, the arrival at Prajñāpāramitā is the Great Divine Mantra; it belongs to the section on the True Doctrine (*saddharma*). It is precisely through the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) that the mind is realized, which differs from the teachings for the Śrāvakas.
The subsequent recitation of the mantra-text is intended for the section on Dissemination (*pravartana*). Indeed, this dissemination is not like that of other sūtras;
for the formless Prajñā cannot be praised, explained, or upheld through words and letters. It is directly within the wordless and...
It is said: "Without thought and without interpretation, one attains silent resonance prior to words and realizes the essence beyond phenomena.
This is what constitutes the true propagation of Prajñā and the authentic transmission of the orthodox lineage; therefore, the secret mantra is proclaimed at the end of the sutra.

The Prajñāpāramitā scriptures comprise more than six hundred fascicles; yet this one alone is titled the *Heart Sūtra* because it does not expound upon the branches and leaves, but speaks solely of the root.
Master Xuanzang was the patriarch of both the Characteristics (Xiang) and Nature (Xing) schools.

Regarding the school of Characteristics, he compiled a hundred fascicles, yet he translated this single fascicle alone to sweep away all phenomenal marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and speak exclusively of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). This is Mañjuśrī.

Regarding the "Gate of Wisdom": Why is it that Avalokiteśvara is mentioned first? It is precisely because when the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they do so solely for the sake of delivering sentient beings from suffering.
If one does not give rise to the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), then even if one possesses fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*), one will be unable to save even oneself.
Avalokiteśvara is the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion who delivers others from suffering and distress; therefore, he is mentioned first as the wondrous wisdom of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
...an exemplary model.
This sutra has been translated six times in total. First, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitāmahāmantra-sūtra*, translated by Kumārajīva during the Yaoqin period of the Eastern Jin dynasty.
Second, the *Prajñāpāramitā* [translated] by Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty.
1. *Bhadra-cittā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Translated during the Three Tang [periods] by Liyan. Its title is identical to that of the translation by Master Xuanzang.
2. Translated during the Song dynasty by Dharmākara. Titled *Samantaprajñājñānagarbha-prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. 3. Translated during the Song dynasty by Dānapāla.
Titled: *The Sūtra on the Perfection of Wisdom, the Mother of the Buddhas Spoken by the Buddha*.
Translated by Dru Dar ma grags. Titled: *The Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom, the Holy Mother of the Bhagavatī*.

Ancient tradition relates that when Master Xuanzang reached the kingdom of Kaśmīra, the path was perilous. While lodging in an empty room, he suddenly heard a monk orally transmit the Heart Sūtra to him.
Consequently, he was able to subdue tigers and leopards and avoid malevolent spirits; thus he reached the Western Regions.
"O Worthy One! This sutra is said to have been taught by Śākyamuni Buddha. Xuánzàng says: "This was spoken by the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
Shīhù’s original version states: "The World-Honored One was on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa;
having entered the profound radiance and finished proclaiming the samādhi, Śāriputra addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: 'If...'"
If there are those who wish to practice and study this profound Dharma-gate of Prajñāpāramitā, how should they practice and study it?

Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva has spoken this sutra; as this sutra is the essential core of the Great Chapter (Mahāprajñāpāramitā) taught by the World-Honored One, one should know that what the Bodhisattva speaks is precisely the word of the World-Honored One. "Avalokiteśvara" means "Contemplating the World."

Avalokiteśvara. First, the etymology; second, the clarification of the essence; third, the elucidation of the principle; fourth, the discussion of the function; fifth, the determination of the characteristics of the teaching.

Now, the title takes the dharma and its metaphor as its name; ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*) as its essence; contemplative observation as its principle; the deliverance from suffering as its function; and the Mahāyāna as...

Regarding the classification of the teachings: appended to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*’s "Investigation of the Mind in Seven Locations," the three contemplations are first presented as the fundamental basis for opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Next, he refutes the false mind as not being within. Rather, the spirit of knowing resides at the gates of the six sense organs;
it is luminously unobscured and clearly aware at all times. Second, he eliminates the attachment that the mind exists outside.
Third, the refutation that the mind does not follow the sense faculties: if the mind were to see mountains and rivers, it should also see the eye.
If the mind were able to see the eye, then the eye would instead become an object perceived by the mind, rather than being the faculty capable of producing perception.
Fourth, the refutation that seeing darkness does not constitute seeing within: when one closes the eyes and sees darkness, it is called "looking back into the body.
If this were the case, then when opening the eyes and seeing light, one should likewise look back at one's own face. If one does not see one's face, then internal facing is not established.
Fifth, the refutation of the mind not being conjoined [with its object]: This means that while dharmas possess a determinate characteristic, the mind lacks a determinate substance.
Since it lacks a determinate substance, there is no locus for conjunction.
Sixth, the refutation based on grasping at an interval: First, one must examine whether the interval exists within the body or within the object; subsequently, both are refuted.
Among these, none have a fixed location.

Seventh, refuting attachment: when the World-Honored One was in the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, he expounded the true doctrine of non-attachment—that [the mind] is neither internal, external, nor in between;
he spoke precisely of the mind having no place of abode. Since there is no place where the mind dwells, one should not further harbor any attachment.

The Dharma-body has no location, yet there is nowhere it is not. At first, Ānanda reckoned that the mind was either inside or outside, or that it resided secretly within the sense organs, or that it was found by combining these two positions, or in the space between them;
thus, he held that the mind had a location. Therefore, the World-Honored One refuted this by means of "having no location.
When he reached the seventh stage, he again reckoned that the mind had no location; the World-Honored One then countered that if there are characteristics, then there must be a location.
He refutes [these views] to collectively reveal the principle that there is neither "being present" nor "not being present.
Among the Tathāgata’s ten great disciples:
Kāśyapa was foremost in asceticism (*dhūta*); Ānanda in erudition; Śāriputra in wisdom; Maudgalyāyana in supernormal powers; and Rāhula...
Pratimokṣa was foremost in ascetic practices; Aniruddha in the divine eye; Pūrṇa in preaching the Dharma; Kātyāyana in expounding the meaning of the teachings;
Upāli in upholding the Vinaya; and Subhūti in understanding emptiness—all were acclaimed as the foremost in their respective fields.
It is traditionally said that within the trichiliocosm, Mount Sumeru constitutes the center.

It is divided into four great continents—Jambudvīpa in the south, Pūrvavideha in the east, Aparagoyānī in the west, and Uttarakuru in the north. Each continent is further divided into eight regions. Furthermore...
There is one medium chiliocosm, which constitutes the realm of the Trāyastriṃśa gods—that is, the Heaven of the Thirty-three—forming a single small world-system (*sāhasracūḍika-lokadhātu*).
One thousand such small world-systems are called a small chiliocosm (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*). One thousand such small chiliocosms are called a medium chiliocosm (*dvisāhasra-madhyama-lokadhātu*).
Again, one thousand such medium chiliocosms are called a great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*). It is because the word "thousand" is stated three times that it is so named.
This refers to the trichiliocosm. The sun and moon reach the midpoint of this mountain and travel around it;
where they shine, it is day, and where they turn their backs, it is night.

Having attained *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), one has reached the further shore and transcended saṃsāra; this is the ultimate stage of cultivation. There are three kinds of "remainder":

first, the remainder of afflictions (*kleśa-śeṣa*); second, the remainder of karma (*karma-śeṣa*); and third, the remainder of karmic fruition (*vipāka-śeṣa*). This is not easily [attained] by those of the Great Vehicle or the Supreme Vehicle.
...attaining this.

First, the Śrāvaka Vehicle: Arhats who have attained the Way rely entirely upon the instructions of the Buddha’s words. Second, the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle: the [Pratyekabuddhas]—*Note: The source text appears to be truncated here.*
The Pratyekabuddhas attain the Way through a sense of resonance that triggers mental awakening.

As for the three Bodhisattva vehicles, they do not merely practice the six perfections but cultivate all myriad practices, with their resolve set upon universal salvation; this constitutes ascending to the Mahāyāna.
Of the six perfections:
first, giving, is the *dāna-pāramitā*; second, ethical discipline, is the *śīla-pāramitā*;
third, patience, is the *kṣānti-pāramitā*; fourth, diligence, is the *vīrya-pāramitā*; fifth, meditative concentration...
Concentration constitutes the dhyāna-pāramitā; the six types of wisdom constitute the prajñā-pāramitā. When these six are complete, one ascends to the other shore;
therefore, they are called the "six perfections" (ṣaṭpāramitā).

The ten stages are as follows: first, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), wherein one attains the realm of the Buddha; second, the Stage of Purity (*vimalā-bhūmi*), wherein the nature of identity and difference is extinguished;

third, the Stage of Radiance (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*), wherein supreme purity gives rise to brilliance; fourth, the Stage of Manifest Wisdom (*arcismatī-bhūmi*), wherein supreme clarity fills with light; fifth, the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), wherein identity and difference... [is transcended].
The Stage of Non-arising; the Stage of Difficult to Conquer, wherein the nature is pure, luminous, and manifest; the Stage of Far-reaching, which reaches the limit of true suchness;
the Stage of Immovability, which unites with the mind of true suchness; the Stage of Good Wisdom, which brings forth the function of true suchness; and the Stage of Clouds of Compassion.
